title: Why Spicy Food Feels Like It's Burning You
topic: Capsaicin activates the TRPV1 heat receptor, so the brain reports fire at body temperature

narration.text: Your mouth isn't actually on fire.
Chili peppers contain capsaicin, a molecule that hijacks your heat sensors.
Those sensors, called TRPV1, normally fire when something hits about forty-three degrees Celsius.
Capsaicin switches them on at body temperature.
So your brain gets one message: fire.
Your body tries to cool a fire that isn't there. You sweat, you flush, your nose runs.
Heat is measured in Scoville units. A jalapeño reaches about eight thousand. The hottest peppers top two million.
Water just spreads capsaicin around. Milk works better: its proteins and fat pull it away.
And birds can't feel it at all, so they eat the peppers and spread the seeds.
What's the hottest thing you've ever eaten?
